speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are experiencing episodes of dizziness and vertigo; can you describe exactly what these sensations feel like to you?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. You mentioned the dizziness is position-dependent and you have a history of hearing loss; does this spinning sensation occur when you roll over in bed, look up, or lean to one side?

REQUEST TEST: Audiometry
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Internal_Auditory_Canals

speaker: Measurement
text:
RESULTS: 
Audiometry: Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, consistent with presbycusis. No sudden drops in hearing indicative of Meniere's disease or labyrinthitis.
MRI_Internal_Auditory_Canals: No evidence of central lesions, infarcts, or structural abnormalities within the internal auditory canals.

speaker: Doctor
text: Those test results are reassuring and help rule out central causes and Meniere's disease. Have these episodes lasted only seconds to a minute, and does the spinning stop completely when you hold your head still?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

The clinical presentation of short-lasting, position-dependent vertigo in an elderly patient with no central signs or other inner ear pathology is classic for BPPV. This is a very common condition in your age group. Are you experiencing any nausea or difficulty walking during these episodes?
